barriers.description: Data collection was conducted without audio recordings, which reduced data quality and depth available to researchers.
barriers.justification: The absence of audio recordings limited designers' ability to manage user understanding and to evaluate and verify user feedback post-hoc, hindering in-depth qualitative insight and rigorous assessment of participant responses.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Especially working without audio recordings likely has affected data quality and data depth.

barriers.description: The team had difficulty recruiting participants with lower education backgrounds, limiting sample diversity.
barriers.justification: This recruitment constraint hindered designers' ability to gain a representative understanding of the target population and impaired requirements specification and contextual understanding for less-educated user segments.
barriers.reference_excerpt: While a heterogeneous age distribution was achieved, it was especially challenging to recruit participants with a lower education background.

barriers.description: Refugees were not pre-screened for symptoms of distress, so participants may not have matched the app's intended clinical target group.
barriers.justification: Not sampling the intended clinical population constrained the designers' ability to specify accurate user requirements and to evaluate the prototype's suitability and potential health impact for the actual target users.
barriers.reference_excerpt: In addition, the interviewed refugees were not pre-screened for symptoms of distress. Consequently, the feedback does not necessarily originate from the exact target group of the app (i.e., Syrian refugees with increased distress and impaired functioning).

barriers.description: The team used prototyping software rather than a fully functioning app, so interactive exercises and real use could only be simulated.
barriers.justification: Relying on non-functional prototypes limited designers' ability to evaluate interactive features, observe real user behaviour over time, and integrate realistic usability feedback into iteration cycles.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Since the prototyping software was used instead of providing a functioning version of an actual app, certain elements such as the interactive exercises could only be simulated at this stage. In order to receive actual feedback on a working prototype it will be necessary to provide access to a fully functioning version.

barriers.description: Free-list interviews asked respondents to answer for the community, causing some responses to be given as representatives rather than from personal experience.
barriers.justification: This interactional method choice produced secondary/hearsay data that weakened designers' ability to manage deep, personal user understanding and to accurately characterise contexts of use.
barriers.reference_excerpt: In the free list interviews, respondents still answered as representatives of the larger group instead of from a personal standpoint. Consequently, this approach may have introduced themes that were rather based on hearsay than on personal experience.

barriers.description: The planned contact-on-demand e-helper model included a 48-hour response latency that was judged too long and required more efficient e-helper management.
barriers.justification: Operational constraints around e-helper availability and response time limited designers' ability to define acceptable guidance features and specify feasible system requirements, impeding production of an acceptable support model.
barriers.reference_excerpt: the suggested response latency of up to 48 h was universally considered as too long and needs to be reduced, e.g., through more efficient systems for e-helper management.
